LAYOFF / REDUCTION-IN-FORCE SELECTION CRITERIA — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp

SELECTION-CRITERIA DOCUMENTATION
LAYOFF / REDUCTION-IN-FORCE SELECTION CRITERIA — DOCUMENTATION RECORD

Company: Acme Corp
Effective date of workforce reduction: November 1, 2026

Selection criteria applied to identify the positions and employees included in this workforce reduction:
seniority within job classification, documented performance ratings for the prior two review cycles

Adverse-impact analysis: an adverse-impact analysis of the selected group by age was performed prior to finalizing the list

This record documents, as of the date signed below, the criteria Acme Corp applied in selecting employees for this workforce reduction and the status of any adverse-impact analysis performed before the layoff list was finalized.

AGE DISCRIMINATION CAN BE PROVEN WITHOUT PROOF OF INTENT
Federal law does not only forbid an employer from intentionally targeting older workers in a layoff. The Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) separately makes it unlawful for an employer "to limit, segregate, or classify" employees in a way that would deprive or tend to deprive an individual of employment opportunities, or otherwise adversely affect their status as an employee, because of age — language that does not require proof of intent, and that courts and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have read to permit a "disparate impact" theory of age discrimination: a claim that a facially neutral, uniformly applied selection method (for example, a layoff process built around a criterion that is not itself age) had a disproportionate adverse effect on older workers as a group, regardless of the employer's intent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "to limit, segregate, or classify his employees in any way which would deprive or tend to deprive any individual of employment opportunities or otherwise adversely affect his status as an employee, because of such individual’s age"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 623(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Age Discrimination in Employment Act, unlawful employer practices (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/623)
  Known gap: This clause's description of disparate-impact theory under the ADEA rests on well-known, publicly reported background about Smith v. City of Jackson, 544 U.S. 228 (2005), in which the U.S. Supreme Court held that the ADEA authorizes disparate-impact claims. That description could not be independently verified against the Court's own opinion text in this research session: CourtListener, the primary-source case-law tool this corpus otherwise uses, returned a rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) when queried for this case, and no quote from the opinion is offered here as a result — consistent with this document's practice of not presenting an unverified citation as verified. The statutory text quoted above (29 U.S.C. § 623(a)(2)) was independently verified by two separate fetches of the U.S. Code from law.cornell.edu, made with distinct User-Agent headers (Chrome/Windows and Safari/Mac) on 2026-09-02, and confirmed textually identical both times. Separately, and importantly: recognizing that a disparate-impact theory exists under the ADEA is not the same as saying such a claim is easy to win. As described in the next clause of this document, the ADEA gives an employer a defense — that the differentiation was based on reasonable factors other than age — that has no identical counterpart under Title VII's disparate-impact framework, and the scope of that defense is a central, separate legal question this clause does not resolve. This document is informational only. It does not determine whether any specific selection method a specific employer used or is considering would, if challenged, be found to have an unlawful disparate impact, and it does not itself state a rule of any state law.

THE "REASONABLE FACTORS OTHER THAN AGE" DEFENSE
The ADEA itself states a defense specific to age-based claims: it is not unlawful for an employer to take an action otherwise prohibited by the statute "where the differentiation is based on reasonable factors other than age." This "RFOA" defense sits alongside, but is textually and legally distinct from, Title VII's business-necessity defense to a race or sex disparate-impact claim — the two statutes use different words for the standard an employer's justification must meet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "or where the differentiation is based on reasonable factors other than age"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 623(f)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Age Discrimination in Employment Act, reasonable-factors-other-than-age defense (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/623)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subsection (29 U.S.C. § 623(f)(1)); no additional independent source is cited for this specific point beyond it. The regulatory content of what "reasonable" requires under this defense — the factors the EEOC looks to in deciding whether a differentiation was based on reasonable factors other than age — is addressed in the next clause of this document, sourced from the EEOC's regulation at 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7, not from the statute quoted here. This document does not determine whether a reasonable-factors-other-than-age defense would succeed for any specific employer's specific layoff selection method; whether it succeeds turns on the particular facts and circumstances of that layoff, which this document does not evaluate. This document is informational only.

WHAT "REASONABLE" MEANS UNDER THE RFOA DEFENSE
The EEOC's regulation interpreting the reasonable-factors-other-than-age defense defines a reasonable factor other than age as "a non-age factor that is objectively reasonable when viewed from the position of a prudent employer mindful of its responsibilities under the ADEA under like circumstances," decided on the particular facts of each situation. To establish the defense, the regulation states that an employer must show the practice was both reasonably designed to further a legitimate business purpose and administered in a way that reasonably achieves that purpose given what the employer knew or should have known. The regulation lists several considerations relevant to that inquiry, including but not limited to: the extent to which the factor relates to the employer's stated business purpose; the extent to which the employer defined and applied the factor accurately and fairly, including whether managers were trained to apply it and avoid discrimination; the extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria involved are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes; the extent to which the employer assessed the adverse impact of the practice on older workers; and the degree of harm to the affected age group, including whether the employer took steps to reduce that harm.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A reasonable factor other than age is a non-age factor that is objectively reasonable when viewed from the position of a prudent employer mindful of its responsibilities under the ADEA under like circumstances."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(1) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, definition of a reasonable factor other than age (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1625.7)
  "To establish the RFOA defense, an employer must show that the employment practice was both reasonably designed to further or achieve a legitimate business purpose and administered in a way that reasonably achieves that purpose in light of the particular facts and circumstances that were known, or should have been known, to the employer."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(1) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, standard for establishing the RFOA defense (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1625.7)
  "(i) The extent to which the factor is related to the employer's stated business purpose; (ii) The extent to which the employer defined the factor accurately and applied the factor fairly and accurately, including the extent to which managers and supervisors were given guidance or training about how to apply the factor and avoid discrimination; (iii) The extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria that the supervisors were asked to evaluate are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes; (iv) The extent to which the employer assessed the adverse impact of its employment practice on older workers; and (v) The degree of the harm to individuals within the protected age group, in terms of both the extent of injury and the numbers of persons adversely affected, and the extent to which the employer took steps to reduce the harm, in light of the burden of undertaking such steps."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, non-exhaustive list of relevant considerations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1625.7)

The regulation itself states that no single consideration is required to be present, and that the presence of one does not automatically establish the defense — this document does not weigh those considerations against one another for any specific employer's specific layoff. Both quotations were independently verified by two separate fetches of this regulation from law.cornell.edu, made with distinct User-Agent headers (Chrome/Windows and Safari/Mac) on 2026-09-02, and confirmed textually identical both times. This document is informational only. It does not determine whether any specific factor a specific employer used to select employees for layoff is, in fact, reasonable, and it does not itself perform the fact-specific weighing the regulation calls for.

CALIFORNIA'S PARALLEL RULE FOR AGE-BASED LAYOFFS
California's own employment discrimination statute, the Fair Employment and Housing Act, does not stop at forbidding intentional age discrimination. By statute, the California Legislature has expressly declared "its intent that the use of salary as the basis for differentiating between employees when terminating employment may be found to constitute age discrimination if use of that criterion adversely impacts older workers as a group," and further declared its intent "that the disparate impact theory of proof may be used in claims of age discrimination" — language enacted specifically to address layoff-type terminations built around a criterion, such as salary, that is not itself age but that can correlate with it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The Legislature declares its intent that the use of salary as the basis for differentiating between employees when terminating employment may be found to constitute age discrimination if use of that criterion adversely impacts older workers as a group, and further declares its intent that the disparate impact theory of proof may be used in claims of age discrimination."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12941 (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Employment and Housing Act, legislative declaration on disparate-impact age claims (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12941.)
  "The Legislature hereby declares its rejection of the court of appeal opinion in Marks v. Loral Corp. (1997) 57 Cal.App.4th 30, and states that the opinion does not affect existing law in any way, including, but not limited to, the law pertaining to disparate treatment."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 12941 (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Fair Employment and Housing Act, legislative rejection of Marks v. Loral Corp. (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12941.)

Code § 12941) was enacted for the specific purpose of legislatively overriding a California Court of Appeal decision, Marks v. Loral Corp. (1997) 57 Cal.App.4th 30, which had held disparate-impact theory unavailable for age claims under California law; the statute's own text states the Legislature's "rejection" of that opinion. This document was not able to independently verify the Marks opinion's own reasoning against a primary source — the same CourtListener rate-limit that affected this document's federal case research (see the ADEA disparate-impact clause above) applies equally to California case law, and no quotation from Marks is offered as a result. Beyond the Legislature's own statement of intent quoted above, this document did not independently verify any specific California appellate decision applying disparate-impact theory to a group layoff's age composition; if such case law exists and would apply to a specific employer's specific layoff, this document does not identify or evaluate it. This statute is one state's law, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's specific layoff, and not a claim that every state recognizes the same theory under its own anti-discrimination statute. This document is informational only.

STATISTICAL ANALYSIS OF A PROPOSED LAYOFF LIST
Because the RFOA defense described earlier in this document turns partly on "the extent to which the employer assessed the adverse impact of its employment practice on older workers," employers conducting a group layoff commonly compare the age composition (and sometimes the composition by other protected characteristics) of the group of employees selected for layoff against the group retained, before the layoff list is finalized — a statistical check against the specific legal risk described in the clauses above, not a step required by any single, universally applicable numeric formula.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The extent to which the employer assessed the adverse impact of its employment practice on older workers"
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2)(iv) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, adverse-impact assessment as a reasonableness factor (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1625.7)
  "A selection rate for any race, sex, or ethnic group which is less than four-fifths ( 4/5 ) (or eighty percent) of the rate for the group with the highest rate will generally be regarded by the Federal enforcement agencies as evidence of adverse impact"
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1607.4(D) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Code of Federal Regulations, Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, the "four-fifths rule" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1607.4)
  Known gap: This clause draws its statistical-analysis framing from one specific EEOC consideration under the ADEA's own regulation, quoted above (29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2)(iv)) — it does not restate the full reasonableness-factors clause and should be read alongside it, not as an independent regulatory source. A correction to a common assumption worth stating directly: the EEOC's separate, frequently cited "four-fifths rule" for measuring adverse impact statistically — a selection rate for one group that is less than four-fifths of the rate for the group with the highest rate is generally regarded as evidence of adverse impact — comes from a different regulation, the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures at 29 C.F.R. § 1607.4(D), and that regulation's own text defines the rule by reference to "race, sex, or ethnic group," not age. This document did not find, within 29 C.F.R. part 1625 (the ADEA-specific regulations), an EEOC adoption of the four-fifths rule as the specific numeric test for an age-based disparate-impact claim; the four-fifths figure is cited here only as background on a widely used general statistical benchmark, not as a rule this document confirms applies, by its own terms, to age. This document does not perform, or instruct the reader to perform, any statistical analysis of any specific layoff list, and does not state what result such an analysis would need to show to avoid liability in a specific case. This document is informational only.

SUBJECTIVE VERSUS OBJECTIVE SELECTION CRITERIA
The EEOC's own regulation interpreting the reasonable-factors-other-than-age defense singles out, as one consideration relevant to whether a layoff-selection factor was reasonable, "the extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria that the supervisors were asked to evaluate are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes." More broadly, and consistent with that regulatory focus, subjective or discretionary selection criteria for a layoff (such as an individual supervisor's unstructured judgment about who is a stronger performer) are generally described by courts and the EEOC as carrying higher discrimination-claim risk than objective, uniformly applied criteria (such as seniority or a documented performance-rating system applied consistently across the workforce) — because subjective criteria are harder to defend against a claim that they were a pretext for a discriminatory reason, and easier for a claimant to second-guess after the fact.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria that the supervisors were asked to evaluate are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes"
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2)(iii) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, supervisor discretion and subjective assessment as a reasonableness factor (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1625.7)
  Known gap: This document verified the quoted regulatory language directly (29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2)(iii)); the broader statement that courts and the EEOC generally draw this subjective/objective distinction reflects a widely reported pattern in employment-discrimination law, not a single additional primary source independently fetched and quoted in this research session — this corpus's CourtListener case-law tool was rate-limited (125 requests/day exhausted) at the time of this research, so no case citation is offered for that broader pattern beyond the one regulation quoted. Describing subjective criteria as carrying comparatively higher risk is not a statement that subjective criteria are unlawful, or that objective criteria are automatically lawful — an objective criterion, including a facially neutral one like seniority or salary, can itself produce an unlawful disparate impact, as described elsewhere in this document. This document does not recommend which selection criteria a specific employer should use for a specific layoff, and does not evaluate whether any specific criteria a specific employer has used or is considering would withstand a discrimination challenge. This document is informational only.

CONNECTION TO THE GROUP-TERMINATION RELEASE DISCLOSURE RULE
The selection-criteria risk described throughout this document connects directly to a separate federal disclosure duty that arises only if a release of claims is used in connection with a group layoff: under the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act, if a release of age-discrimination claims is requested in connection with an exit-incentive or other employment-termination program offered to a group or class of employees, the employer must inform each individual in writing, at the start of the consideration period, of the job titles and ages of everyone eligible or selected for the program, and the ages of everyone in the same job classification or organizational unit who was not eligible or selected. In practice, that disclosure obligation puts the very same age composition of the selected-versus-not-selected group described earlier in this document directly in front of the employees being asked to sign a release.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "if a waiver is requested in connection with an exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class of employees, the employer (at the commencement of the period specified in subparagraph (F)) informs the individual in writing in a manner calculated to be understood by the average individual eligible to participate, as to— (i) any class, unit, or group of individuals covered by such program, any eligibility factors for such program, and any time limits applicable to such program; and (ii) the job titles and ages of all individuals eligible or selected for the program, and the ages of all individuals in the same job classification or organizational unit who are not eligible or selected for the program."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(H) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Older Workers Benefit Protection Act, group-termination disclosure requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/626)

This clause does not re-derive that requirement; it exists only to connect this document's layoff-selection-criteria topic to that separately covered disclosure duty, for a reader using both documents together. The quotation below was independently re-verified for this document by two separate fetches of 29 U.S.C. § 626 from law.cornell.edu, made with distinct User-Agent headers (Chrome/Windows and Safari/Mac) on 2026-09-02, and confirmed textually identical both times, rather than simply copied forward from the earlier document's research. This disclosure duty applies only when a release of claims is being requested in connection with a group program — it does not apply to a layoff where no release is used, and this document does not determine whether any specific layoff involves the kind of "exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class of employees" that triggers it. This document is informational only.

The undersigned, Jordan Alex Lee, VP of Human Resources of Acme Corp, certifies that the selection-criteria documentation above accurately describes, to the best of the undersigned's knowledge, the criteria Acme Corp applied in this workforce reduction and the status of any adverse-impact analysis performed.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause draws its statistical-analysis framing from one specific EEOC consideration under the ADEA's own regulation, quoted above (29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2)(iv)) — it does not restate the full reasonableness-factors clause and should be read alongside it, not as an independent regulatory source. A correction to a common assumption worth stating directly: the EEOC's separate, frequently cited "four-fifths rule" for measuring adverse impact statistically — a selection rate for one group that is less than four-fifths of the rate for the group with the highest rate is generally regarded as evidence of adverse impact — comes from a different regulation, the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures at 29 C.F.R. § 1607.4(D), and that regulation's own text defines the rule by reference to "race, sex, or ethnic group," not age. This document did not find, within 29 C.F.R. part 1625 (the ADEA-specific regulations), an EEOC adoption of the four-fifths rule as the specific numeric test for an age-based disparate-impact claim; the four-fifths figure is cited here only as background on a widely used general statistical benchmark, not as a rule this document confirms applies, by its own terms, to age. This document does not perform, or instruct the reader to perform, any statistical analysis of any specific layoff list, and does not state what result such an analysis would need to show to avoid liability in a specific case. This document is informational only.

expectedJSON.body: The EEOC's own regulation interpreting the reasonable-factors-other-than-age defense singles out, as one consideration relevant to whether a layoff-selection factor was reasonable, "the extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria that the supervisors were asked to evaluate are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes." More broadly, and consistent with that regulatory focus, subjective or discretionary selection criteria for a layoff (such as an individual supervisor's unstructured judgment about who is a stronger performer) are generally described by courts and the EEOC as carrying higher discrimination-claim risk than objective, uniformly applied criteria (such as seniority or a documented performance-rating system applied consistently across the workforce) — because subjective criteria are harder to defend against a claim that they were a pretext for a discriminatory reason, and easier for a claimant to second-guess after the fact.

citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, supervisor discretion and subjective assessment as a reasonableness factor
citations.quote: The extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria that the supervisors were asked to evaluate are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes

expectedJSON.gap: This document verified the quoted regulatory language directly (29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2)(iii)); the broader statement that courts and the EEOC generally draw this subjective/objective distinction reflects a widely reported pattern in employment-discrimination law, not a single additional primary source independently fetched and quoted in this research session — this corpus's CourtListener case-law tool was rate-limited (125 requests/day exhausted) at the time of this research, so no case citation is offered for that broader pattern beyond the one regulation quoted. Describing subjective criteria as carrying comparatively higher risk is not a statement that subjective criteria are unlawful, or that objective criteria are automatically lawful — an objective criterion, including a facially neutral one like seniority or salary, can itself produce an unlawful disparate impact, as described elsewhere in this document. This document does not recommend which selection criteria a specific employer should use for a specific layoff, and does not evaluate whether any specific criteria a specific employer has used or is considering would withstand a discrimination challenge. This document is informational only.

expectedJSON.body: The selection-criteria risk described throughout this document connects directly to a separate federal disclosure duty that arises only if a release of claims is used in connection with a group layoff: under the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act, if a release of age-discrimination claims is requested in connection with an exit-incentive or other employment-termination program offered to a group or class of employees, the employer must inform each individual in writing, at the start of the consideration period, of the job titles and ages of everyone eligible or selected for the program, and the ages of everyone in the same job classification or organizational unit who was not eligible or selected. In practice, that disclosure obligation puts the very same age composition of the selected-versus-not-selected group described earlier in this document directly in front of the employees being asked to sign a release.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, Older Workers Benefit Protection Act, group-termination disclosure requirement
citations.quote: if a waiver is requested in connection with an exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class of employees, the employer (at the commencement of the period specified in subparagraph (F)) informs the individual in writing in a manner calculated to be understood by the average individual eligible to participate, as to— (i) any class, unit, or group of individuals covered by such program, any eligibility factors for such program, and any time limits applicable to such program; and (ii) the job titles and ages of all individuals eligible or selected for the program, and the ages of all individuals in the same job classification or organizational unit who are not eligible or selected for the program.

expectedJSON.gap: This is the same federal statutory provision, 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(H), already covered in full — along with the OWBPA's other release requirements, its 21-day/45-day and 7-day timing rules, and its EEOC-participation carve-out — by this corpus's Severance Agreement document, in the clause titled "Age Discrimination Release Requirements" (clause id sev_owbpa). This clause does not re-derive that requirement; it exists only to connect this document's layoff-selection-criteria topic to that separately covered disclosure duty, for a reader using both documents together. The quotation below was independently re-verified for this document by two separate fetches of 29 U.S.C. § 626 from law.cornell.edu, made with distinct User-Agent headers (Chrome/Windows and Safari/Mac) on 2026-09-02, and confirmed textually identical both times, rather than simply copied forward from the earlier document's research. This disclosure duty applies only when a release of claims is being requested in connection with a group program — it does not apply to a layoff where no release is used, and this document does not determine whether any specific layoff involves the kind of "exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class of employees" that triggers it. This document is informational only.
